description: The image presents three side-by-side bar charts labeled (a) WikiText, (b) an unlabeled dataset (with a gray placeholder title), and (c) C4, each comparing the perplexity performance of two quantization methods — “Uniform” (blue bars) and “Ours” (orange bars) — across four levels of quantization bits: 3, 4, 8, and 16. In all three charts, the vertical axis represents “Perplexity” with a linear scale ranging from 0 to a maximum that varies per chart: approximately 30 in (a) and (c), and 400 in (b). The horizontal axis is labeled “Quantization Bits” and displays the four discrete bit-widths. In chart (a) WikiText, “Uniform” achieves perplexities of ~29, ~27, ~26.5, and ~26.5 for 3, 4, 8, and 16 bits respectively, while “Ours” achieves ~21.5, ~19, ~18.2, and ~18.2 — showing consistently lower (better) perplexity. In chart (b), “Uniform” scores ~405, ~315, ~300, and ~300, while “Ours” scores ~245, ~180, ~185, and ~185 — again, “Ours” is significantly better, especially at lower bit-widths. In chart (c) C4, “Uniform” scores ~28, ~25, ~24.5, and ~24.5, while “Ours” scores ~20.5, ~18, ~17.7, and ~17.7 — again demonstrating superior performance. Across all datasets, “Ours” consistently outperforms “Uniform” in perplexity, with the largest gains observed at lower bit-widths (e.g., 3 and 4 bits), and performance differences narrowing as bit-width increases. The bars are grouped by bit-width, with “Uniform” always to the left of “Ours” within each group, and no error bars or additional annotations are present.
